question: Across the world, men’s mental health is emerging as a distinct area requiring action, as social norms have a profound influence on emotional expression, hindering the search for help. The World Psychiatric Association supports the implementation of specific policies on men’s mental health. Australia is implementing a national men’s health strategy, which focuses on suicide prevention and addressing stigma.

Organisations such as Movember are active globally. In Canada, policy analysis on gender has led to male identity being incorporated into mental health services. The Canadian Men’s Health Network promotes targeted action. In the United Kingdom, organisations such as CALM and parliamentary committees examine the relationship between masculinity and mental health.

In 2018, the American Psychological Association issued guidance for psychological practice with boys and men, promoting male support networks. The Commission has presented a strategic framework of 20 flagship initiatives (2023) with EUR 1.

23 billion funding, aiming at: — preventing depression and suicide (80 % of suicides are committed by men); — raising awareness and improving access to high-quality mental health services; — creating a European Depression and Suicide Prevention Initiative with EUR 6 million for prevention measures and exchange of good practices; — developing a European Code for Mental Health (EUR 2 million) to provide guidance. 1.
How does the Commission assess the implementation of the framework?
Has it discerned best practices from some Member States?
What steps does it think should be taken in order to make progress in the area of men’s mental health?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2025) In 2023 the Commission adopted the Communication on a comprehensive approach to mental health1. It supports Member States and stakeholders in addressing mental health issues through 20 flagship initiatives and almost EUR 1.3 million in funding opportunities. The Commission monitors the implementation of the Communication through a tracking framework2.

Some of these flagship initiatives include a project with the World Health Organisation3 to provide Member States targeted support via policy dialogues and capacity building to improve their mental health systems, a multi-disciplinary training and exchange programme for health professionals4 and an EU support package on stigma and discrimination.

The focus of the Communication is on supporting vulnerable population groups, such as children, young people and older persons. The 2024 EU4Health Work Programme5,6 includes a grant to Member States and a call for proposals to stakeholders to support a comprehensive, prevention-oriented approach to mental health of vulnerable groups.

The 2025 EU4Health Work Programme7 includes a call for proposals on lifelong prevention for a healthy life with a focus on cardiovascular diseases, which will also address mental health. Following the adoption of the Communication, the Commission launched a call for Member States and stakeholders to submit best and promising practices on mental health8.

29 initiatives were identified and uploaded to the EU Best Practice Portal on Public Health9. These proven and concrete practices are publicly available, and Member States may choose to transfer (elements of) them at national, regional or local level. The Commission consults with Member States via the Public Health Expert Group10 on public health priorities.
